pdf.title: NCERT Class 9 Contemporary India–I · Chapter 4: Climate

meta.subject: Geography
meta.title: Climate
meta.intro: The difference between weather and climate, climatic controls, the monsoon mechanism, India’s four seasons, rainfall distribution and the influence of climate on life.

objectives: Explain climate using geographical concepts and Indian examples.
Identify the important terms, patterns, processes and locations in this chapter.
Interpret maps, tables and geographical evidence.
Connect the chapter with human life, environment and regional development.

blocks.text: Weather is the state of the atmosphere over a place at a particular time. Climate is the average pattern of weather conditions and their variations over a large area for a long period, conventionally around 30 years or more.
The main elements of weather and climate are temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity and precipitation. Weather may change within hours, while climate describes longer-term patterns.
A seasonal reversal in the direction of prevailing winds, associated with seasonal differences in heating and pressure between land and sea.
India has a monsoon-type climate, but temperature and rainfall vary widely from region to region because of latitude, altitude, relief, distance from the sea and atmospheric circulation.

sections.title: Climatic Controls and Factors Affecting India

blocks.text: The six major controls of climate are latitude, altitude, pressure and wind system, distance from the sea, ocean currents and relief features.

Latitude affects the angle and intensity of solar energy. Altitude generally lowers temperature with increasing height. Coastal areas experience a moderating influence from the sea, while interiors often have greater seasonal temperature extremes.

Pressure and wind systems transport heat and moisture. Ocean currents can warm or cool nearby coasts when onshore winds carry their influence inland. Mountains can block winds, force air to rise and produce orographic rainfall.

rows: Blocks winds and creates rain shadows

blocks.text: During summer, intense heating creates low pressure over northwestern India and adjoining interior Asia. The Indian Ocean remains relatively higher in pressure, encouraging moisture-bearing winds to move towards the subcontinent.

Southeast trade winds from the southern hemisphere cross the Equator and are deflected to the right by the Coriolis force. They reach India as the southwest monsoon and split into the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches.

The Arabian Sea branch gives heavy rainfall along the windward side of the Western Ghats and advances towards northwestern India. The Bay of Bengal branch moves towards northeast India and then westward along the Ganga plains.
The monsoon does not produce continuous rain everywhere. Active and break phases, depressions, local relief and changing circulation create variations in rainfall.

blocks.title: Coriolis force
blocks.text: An apparent deflection caused by Earth’s rotation: moving air is deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

The cold weather season generally extends from mid-November to February in northern India. Northeast trade winds prevail; most regions are dry, but western disturbances bring winter rain to northwestern plains and snowfall in the Himalayas. Tamil Nadu receives some rainfall from northeast winds after they cross the Bay of Bengal.

The hot weather season extends broadly from March to May. Temperatures rise, low pressure develops over northwestern India, and local storms occur. Loo is a hot, dry wind in northern and northwestern India. Pre-monsoon showers benefit parts of southern India.

The advancing southwest monsoon is the main rainy season, broadly from June to September. The monsoon arrives first over the Kerala coast and advances across the country. Rainfall is concentrated in this period for much of India.

The retreating monsoon occurs mainly during October and November. The monsoon withdraws from northwestern India; low-pressure systems and cyclones over the Bay of Bengal can bring rain to the eastern coast, especially Tamil Nadu.

rows: High temperatures, loo and local storms
Withdrawal; cyclonic rain on east coast

sections.title: Distribution of Rainfall and Climate’s Influence

blocks.text: Rainfall is unevenly distributed. The windward Western Ghats and parts of northeastern India receive very heavy rainfall, while western Rajasthan, Ladakh and rain-shadow areas receive much less.

Rainfall generally decreases from east to west across the Northern Plains because the Bay of Bengal branch loses moisture as it travels westward. Coastal areas usually have a smaller annual temperature range than inland regions.
Climate influences crops, water availability, housing, clothing, transport, health and livelihoods. Droughts, floods, heat waves, cold waves and cyclones can create serious risks.

blocks.title: Map practice
blocks.text: Mark the Western Ghats, Meghalaya plateau, Thar Desert, Ladakh, Tamil Nadu coast and the broad direction of both southwest monsoon branches.
